title: Infinite Horizon Markov Economies
one_liner: A paper extends game theory to economies where players' choices reshape what other players can do, and solves for equilibrium prices and quantities over infinite time.
lead: Trade and prices seem to emerge from nowhere, but mathematically they must satisfy balance: what one person wants to buy, another wants to sell, and the prices that make this happen are called equilibrium. In complex economies where time matters, people's choices change what options others face, and modeling this requires a new framework called Markov pseudo-games.

problem.h2: Modeling dynamic economies with changing action sets
paras: Economists study markets where people buy, sell, and trade over time under uncertainty (weather, health, job loss). The standard tool, called general equilibrium theory, asks: what prices balance supply and demand so everyone is happy with their choice? But this breaks when time and uncertainty matter together. In real life, if I go bankrupt today, tomorrow I can no longer buy anything—my action set shrinks. Standard equilibrium theory ignores this: it assumes my options today do not change depending on what you do.

A beginner might try to extend equilibrium theory by just adding time, treating each year as a separate market. This fails because it misses how today's bankruptcy ripples forward: if I know I might have no buying power tomorrow, I save differently today. The real problem is that the paper needs a single framework that captures time, uncertainty, and the fact that one player's action shapes another player's choices—all at once.

callout.html: How do you prove equilibrium exists when players' available actions depend on what other players do?

steps.text: Rewrite the market so when player A chooses, it shrinks player B's available options.
Track wealth and holdings as a state; equilibrium looks backward at history.
Adapt the economist's Radner equilibrium to infinite time.
Show a first-order method (gradient-based nudging) reaches equilibrium in polynomial time.
Use a generative adversarial policy network to approximate the price function.

paras: The paper redefines the core object: instead of a static market where everyone's actions are independent, it rewrites the game so that one player's choice directly determines which actions the other player can take. In game-theory terms, the 'action set' becomes a function of other players' moves.

hidden.name: equilibrium price sequence
paras: An equilibrium is a sequence of prices over infinite time such that, at each moment, every player is making the best choice given the prices they see and the randomness ahead. The key hidden quantity is the price function itself—a rule that, given the current wealth and holdings, returns the price.

The paper constructs this function by solving a Markov pseudo-game. The function must satisfy a recursive condition: the price today must be consistent with optimal choices today and equilibrium prices tomorrow. This is called a 'fixed point'—a price path that, when players optimize given that path, produces the path itself.

heat.caption: Darker means more tightly linked to the equilibrium prices.

reads.html: The equilibrium price is a rule: given what people own today, what should they pay for one more unit?
The recursive Radner equilibrium is a fixed point of the value function operator, where value(state, action) solves the Bellman equation.

paras: The paper makes three moves. First, it reformulates the economic problem as a game: instead of asking 'what price balances supply and demand,' it asks 'what price-setting strategy is a best response when other players use that strategy too?' This is a fixed-point problem.

Second, it rewrites the action space so that when player A's wealth drops (because they made a bad trade), player B automatically faces fewer options. This is done by making each player's action set a function of the state (wealth, holdings). The paper then proves that in this reformulated game, an equilibrium must exist—a price and quantity sequence nobody wants to deviate from.

Third, the paper shows this fixed point can be found fast. It constructs a concave optimization problem whose solution IS the equilibrium. A first-order method (gradient descent on prices) converges to equilibrium in polynomial time, meaning the algorithm scales to realistic economies. The neural network learns the price function by playing against itself, like an adversary learning to set prices and a player learning to trade optimally.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine two traders, each with 10 units of wheat. State s = (wealth_A=100, wealth_B=100).
Trader A wants to buy if price < 5 per unit (expects rain, higher value tomorrow). Demand D(4,s) = 5 units.
Trader B is pessimistic, wants to sell. Supply S(4,s) = 8 units. Excess supply = 3.
Algorithm raises price to 6, which shifts demand down to 2 and supply to 5. Still unbalanced.
At price 7: demand = 0, supply = 3. Overshoot. Try price 5.5: demand = 2, supply = 4.
After a few iterations, price converges to 5.2. At this price, demand = supply, state clears.

math.note: The price adjusts until the amount buyers want at that price exactly equals the amount sellers want to give up, and this balance holds at every future state.

charts.title: Without interlocked actions (standard model)
charts.note: Standard theory proves existence but leaves algorithms and infinite time as open questions.

charts.title: With Markov pseudo-games (this paper)
charts.note: The paper closes all three gaps at once by reformulating the problem as a game.

items.html: If random events (weather, job loss) are too extreme, the state space explodes and the algorithm becomes slow. The paper assumes shocks are bounded.
If traders cannot insure against all risks (no derivative contracts), there may be many equilibria, not one. The paper assumes sufficient market structure.
When a network learns the price function, it may overshoot and violate constraints (e.g., prices go negative). The paper uses a constrained adversarial training scheme.
When state spaces are tractable and markets are complete, the algorithm provably finds equilibrium in polynomial time.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small two-person infinite-horizon market: both agents hold wheat or money, face random harvests each year, can trade. Initialize prices arbitrarily. Run the gradient-descent algorithm on prices. Plot: (1) price convergence over iterations; (2) supply and demand at each step (they should cross); (3) each agent's total wealth over 50 years (should be stable, not collapse); (4) total demand vs. supply each year (residual should shrink to near-zero). Visualize the state space as a heatmap: how often the algorithm visits each (wealth_A, wealth_B) pair.
demo.closing: The demo must show that prices stop moving and supply equals demand at every step of the 50-year simulation.
